# Hero videos

`hero-desktop.mp4` / `hero-mobile.mp4` and their matching poster JPEGs are
**owner-supplied** assets for the homepage hero (not generated by this
project). They are replaced whenever the owner supplies new footage —
see "Revision history" below. The originals the owner provides are
**not** stored in this repository — they stay wherever the owner keeps
them. The files here are optimized, audio-stripped production copies
only.

## Current revision (2026-09-12)

Owner-supplied originals:

- `desktop hero section.mp4` — 1280×720 (16:9), 24fps, 10.005s,
  H.264 + AAC, 3,634,603 B (3.63 MB)
- `mobile hero section.mp4` — 720×1280 (9:16), 24fps, 10.005s,
  H.264 + AAC, 4,938,078 B (4.94 MB)

Both are a branded "Enveloped" invitation-card animation (embossed
envelope, wax seal, roses, a card reading "Enveloped"), 240 frames at
24fps, landscape and portrait versions of the same scene.

## What was done to produce the optimized copies

1. **Audio removed entirely** (`-an`) — the hero video is decorative,
   autoplaying, muted background media and must never carry or depend on
   an audio track (see `src/components/site/HeroVideo.tsx`'s own
   comment).
2. **Seamless loop point forced.** The owner's source is *not* a
   pixel-identical loop on its own (the ambient petals/sparkles drift
   continuously rather than resetting) — the first and last frames
   measured only ~0.63 SSIM similarity, enough to read as a visible
   "jump" at the loop point. Rather than trim content or accept the
   jump, the encode reuses the source's own frame 0 as the video's
   final frame (an `ffmpeg` `trim`+`concat` filter graph: frames
   0–238 unchanged, frame 239 replaced with a copy of frame 0),
   preserving the full 240-frame/10-second length and virtually all of
   the original motion — only the very last 1/24s frame changes. This
   raises first/last-frame similarity to ~0.98 SSIM (visually seamless;
   the small remainder is ordinary H.264 quantization, since the same
   source pixels still pass through lossy compression twice at two
   different points in the GOP structure).
3. **Re-encoded** H.264 (`-crf 20 -preset slow`, `yuv420p`,
   `-profile:v high -level 4.0`, `+faststart`) — `crf 20` (rather than
   the `23` used for the previous, simpler-textured revision) to keep
   the fine embossed-paper and sparkle detail clean at this content's
   higher visual complexity. `+faststart` moves the `moov` atom to the
   front of the file so playback can begin before the whole file
   downloads.
4. **Poster = the exact first frame** (frame 0) of each optimized
   video, extracted as a high-quality JPEG (`-q:v 2`) — shown
   immediately, kept visible under the video until it's confirmed
   playing, and permanently in place of the video for
   `prefers-reduced-motion` viewers. Using frame 0 exactly (rather than
   a later "calm" frame, as the previous revision did) means the
   poster-to-video handoff is not just similar but pixel-continuous.

Regeneration command (requires `ffmpeg`; run against the owner's current
original if it's ever replaced):

```bash
ffmpeg -i "<original>.mp4" -filter_complex "
[0:v]trim=start_frame=0:end_frame=239,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS[body];
[0:v]trim=start_frame=0:end_frame=1,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS[first];
[body][first]concat=n=2:v=1:a=0[outv]
" -map "[outv]" -an -c:v libx264 -profile:v high -level 4.0 \
  -crf 20 -preset slow -pix_fmt yuv420p -movflags +faststart <output>.mp4

ffmpeg -i <output>.mp4 -vf "select=eq(n\,0)" -vframes 1 -q:v 2 <output>-poster.jpg
```

(If a future source is already an exact frame-for-frame loop, the
`trim`/`concat` step is unnecessary — a plain `-c:v libx264 ...` encode
of the whole file is enough; check with the SSIM command in the
"Verifying a loop" section below before assuming so.)

### Verifying a loop is seamless

```bash
ffmpeg -i <file>.mp4 -vf "select=eq(n\,0)" -vframes 1 first.png
ffmpeg -i <file>.mp4 -vf "select=eq(n\,239)" -vframes 1 last.png   # 239 = frame count - 1
ffmpeg -i first.png -i last.png -lavfi ssim -f null -              # look at the "All:" value
```
`All: 1.0` is pixel-identical; ~`0.98`+ reads as seamless to the eye;
well below that (this project saw ~0.63 on the raw source) is a visible
jump.
